edo_domains: Mito Domain (one of the three Tokugawa houses)

meiji_transition.summary: After 1871 the area was reorganized into Niihari, Ibaraki and Inba prefectures, settling in 1875 as Ibaraki (all of Hitachi plus northern Shimōsa).
meiji_transition.boundary_note: Rerouting the Tone River eastward made it the border with Chiba, so northern Shimōsa (Koga, Yūki, etc.) ended up in Ibaraki.

history_timeline.title: Hitachi no Kuni Fudoki
history_timeline.summary: The Hitachi Fudoki is one of only five surviving provincial gazetteers; Kashima Shrine is the head of the eastern war-god cult.

history_timeline.title: Shinran in Hitachi
history_timeline.summary: Vassals such as the Hitachi Daijō and the Satake were active; Shinran preached for nearly twenty years at his Inada hermitage and wrote the Kyōgyōshinshō.

history_timeline.title: The Jinnō Shōtōki
history_timeline.summary: During the Northern and Southern Courts era Kitabatake Chikafusa held Oda and Seki castles in Hitachi and wrote the Jinnō Shōtōki; the Satake rose as Northern Court governors.

history_timeline.title: Satake, 'Tarō of Bandō'
history_timeline.summary: Satake Yoshishige, called 'Tarō of Bandō', held out against the Later Hōjō and largely unified Hitachi; his son Yoshinobu was moved to Akita in 1602.

history_timeline.title: The Mito school
history_timeline.summary: Tokugawa Mitsukuni began compiling the Dai Nihon-shi, founding the Mito school whose reverence for the emperor shaped the late-Edo 'sonnō jōi' movement.

history_timeline.title: City of science
history_timeline.summary: From the 1960s Tsukuba Science City was built, home to JAXA and other institutes; the Kashima coastal industrial zone grew alongside it.

landmarks.name: Kairakuen
landmarks.note: One of Japan's three great gardens, with 3,000 plum trees

landmarks.name: Kashima Shrine
landmarks.note: One of the three great shrines of the east

specialties.name: Ankō nabe
specialties.note: Monkfish hot pot of the winter Hitachi coast

dialect.name: Ibaraki dialect
dialect.features: An accentless dialect with heavy voicing ('ka' sounds close to 'ga'); thought blunt, but honest at heart.

guide.opening: Meow~ I'm Shōfuku, a cat who escaped from an ukiyo-e print. Mito Kōmon's Dai Nihon-shi took over two hundred years to write — want to hear how it stirred up the end of the shogunate?

regional_meme.title: Last in charm
regional_meme.text: Ibaraki has long ranked last in the 'prefectural attractiveness' survey — and its people have turned that into a running joke.

regional_meme.title: The pronunciation war
regional_meme.text: It's 'Ibaraki', not 'Ibaragi'! Voicing that 'ki' is one of the things Ibaraki people mind most.

hero_persona.name: Tokugawa Mitsukuni
hero_persona.title: Mito Kōmon · compiler of the Dai Nihon-shi
hero_persona.opening_line: I am Mitsukuni of Mito. People say I wandered the provinces in disguise punishing villains — that's theater. The history project, though, is entirely true.
hero_persona.tone_prompt: gentle yet dignified, devoted to scholarship and history; jokes now and then about the TV 'Mito Kōmon'

ramen.toppings: Pumpkin, cabbage and liver stir-fried in a sweet-spicy gravy
ramen.highlight: Hardly any soup — just a big ladle of sweet-spicy 'stamina' gravy on top

sake.taste_profile: Light & dry: an elegant pure-rice sake from one of Japan's oldest breweries
